9 Materials That Help With Functional Communication for SIB
It's 7:43 AM. The task changed without warning. And before you could explain, she had already bitten her hand. She wasn't trying to hurt herself. She was trying to tell you something her words couldn't say.
You are not failing. Her nervous system is speaking — in the only language it currently has. This page gives her a new language. One that doesn't require pain to be heard.

Millions of Parents Are Navigating What You're Navigating Right Now
Your child's self-injury is not random. It is not manipulation. It is not aggression toward you. Across two decades of behavioral science and 20 million therapy sessions, the evidence is consistent: when children lack an efficient, reliable way to communicate an urgent need — they use their bodies. The self-injury is the message. Our task is to give them a better messenger.

PRISMA systematic review (2024): 80% of children diagnosed with autism display sensory processing difficulties. Multiple meta-analyses confirm functional communication training as top-tier evidence-based practice for behavior change. References: PMC11506176 | PMC10955541
Under Stress, the Speaking Brain Goes Offline. The Acting Body Takes Over.
The Neuroscience
When a child with autism faces an overwhelming demand, denied request, or sensory overload, the amygdala (threat-detection center) triggers a cascade that floods the prefrontal cortex with cortisol and adrenaline.
Broca's area — the speech production region — loses executive access. Words that were available at baseline become completely inaccessible. The higher-order communication system literally goes offline. What remains online: the motor system. Hitting, biting, scratching, head-banging — these require no language. They are motor outputs that communicate without words.
For You, the Parent
"Use your words" doesn't work because the words aren't there.
Your child isn't choosing to hurt herself instead of talking. The talk function is temporarily unavailable. The body is the only communication system still operating.
Functional Communication Training (FCT) works because it gives the child communication tools that are simple enough to operate even when the language brain is partially offline: one press, one card, one touch — no sentences required.
"This is a wiring difference under stress, not a behavior choice."

Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020): Sensory and emotional flooding in ASD disrupts language networks while motor systems remain active — the neurological basis for why AAC and communication alternatives must be accessible during distress. DOI: 10.3389/fnint.2020.556660
Your Child Is Here. This Is Where the Journey Leads.
SIB with communicative function most commonly emerges between ages 2–5 in children with limited verbal communication. It does not mean the child "chose" self-harm — it means the child's communication development hit a gap that the behavior filled. FCT closes that gap.

Functional Communication Training: The Most Replicated Behavior Intervention in Autism Science
🏆 Level I — Systematic Review + Multiple RCTs
Highest Evidence Tier | 40+ Years of Replication
FCT Foundational Evidence (1985–present)
Carr & Durand (1985) demonstrated that when children were taught to communicate the same function as their problem behavior, problem behavior decreased by 90%+. This has been replicated across hundreds of studies.
NCAEP Classification (2020)
The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice classifies FCT as a Focused Intervention Practice with the highest evidence designation across multiple age groups and behavioral functions.
SIB-Specific Meta-Analysis
Multiple meta-analyses confirm FCT produces significant, durable reduction in SIB when the communication alternative matches the behavioral function and is honored consistently.
Indian Context
Padmanabha et al., Indian Journal of Pediatrics (2019): Home-based communication interventions in Indian pediatric populations demonstrated significant outcomes when caregivers were trained in consistent response protocols. DOI: 10.1007/s12098-018-2747-4
"Clinically validated. Home-applicable. Parent-proven." FCT is not experimental. It is not alternative. It is the evidence-based standard of care for communicative SIB, endorsed by WHO, UNICEF, NCAEP, and 40+ years of applied behavior analysis research.

Functional Communication Training for Self-Injurious Behavior
Parent-friendly alias: "Giving your child a voice that doesn't require pain"
What FCT Is
Functional Communication Training (FCT) is an evidence-based behavioral intervention that identifies what a child's self-injurious behavior is communicating — escape, attention, a want, an internal state — and teaches a simple, efficient communication replacement that serves the exact same function.
FCT works because it doesn't fight the communication need — it redirects it to a safer, more effective channel.
In Practice
  • Instead of hitting his head to escape a task → child presses a Big Mack button: "I need a break"
  • Instead of biting her hand when overwhelmed → child points to a visual scale showing a 5
  • Instead of scratching to say "I need you" → child taps the caregiver's arm
Badges
  • 📋 Domain: Behavior / Communication / SIB
  • 👶 Age: 2–12 years | ⏱️ Duration: 5–20 min
  • 📅 Frequency: Embedded in ALL daily contexts
  • 📊 Evidence: Level I
"Self-injury works because it communicates. FCT works because it communicates better." — Pinnacle Blooms BCBA Consortium
FCT Requires a Full Consortium. Here's Who Deploys It and How.
ABA / BCBA — Primary Lead
Conducts functional behavior assessment (FBA) to identify SIB function. Designs FCT protocol. Trains caregivers. Monitors data.
Speech-Language Pathology — Co-Lead
Assesses communication modality access. Selects and programs AAC. Designs vocabulary targeting. Monitors communication growth.
Occupational Therapy — Core Support
Assesses motor access to communication devices. Addresses sensory contributors to SIB. Evaluates positioning for AAC use.
Special Education — Core Support
Implements FCT across school environments. Ensures consistency with classroom demands. Caregiver training in educational contexts.
NeuroDev Pediatrics — Safety Gate
Rules out medical causes of SIB (pain, GI, dental, infections). Considers pharmacological supports where needed.
"The brain doesn't organize by therapy type. A child who hurts himself to escape a demand has a behavioral need, a communication need, a sensory need, and potentially a medical need — simultaneously." — Pinnacle FusionModule™ Consortium
📞 9100 181 181
This Is Not a Random Activity. It Is a Precision Communication Tool.
FCT targets behavior change across three concentric rings — from the core SIB outcome outward to long-term self-advocacy and family system relief.
🎯 Primary Target
Reduction of SIB through Functional Communication Replacement. The child uses the assigned communication tool in the context where SIB previously occurred. SIB frequency/intensity decreases within 2–6 weeks of consistent FCT implementation.
Secondary Targets
  • Expressive communication expansion across functions and contexts
  • Caregiver responsiveness increase — faster response latency
  • Emotional regulation scaffolding through visual scales
  • Trust and connection — child-caregiver relationship strengthens
Tertiary Targets
  • Long-term self-advocacy capacity
  • Generalized AAC use across settings and partners
  • School inclusion readiness
  • Family system relief and reduced crisis frequency
Observable Behavior Indicators by Week
Week 1–2
Child contacts or approaches communication tool during distress (even without using it)
Week 3–4
Child uses tool for primary SIB function at least occasionally
Week 5–8
SIB frequency begins measurable decline; communication attempts increase
Week 8+
Communication used across multiple functions; SIB rare outside novel extreme situations

🔴 Material 1
Big Mack / Single-Message Voice Output Device
What It Is
A large, single-button device pre-programmed with one recorded message — "I need a break," "Stop," or "Help me." One press = immediate voice output. Always ready. Always clear.
Canon Category
AAC Materials / Voice Output Devices
Price Range
₹3,000–8,000
Why It Works
Requires minimal motor planning. Always ready. Produces unambiguous output. Can be faster than self-injury — which means it outcompetes the SIB as a communication strategy when honored immediately and consistently.
The Big Mack is the first-line recommendation for escape-maintained and attention-maintained SIB in children ages 2–7.

🟠 Material 2
Visual Break Cards / Stop Signals
What It Is
A laminated card with a clear "BREAK" or "STOP" symbol the child hands to the caregiver to request escape. The physical exchange is the communication act — no speech, no technology required.

Why It Works
Requires no speech, no technology. The physical exchange creates unambiguous communication. Works even in high distress states where device access or verbal output fails.

Core Vocabulary AAC Board
What It Is
A laminated board with 8–16 highest-frequency words — STOP, HELP, MORE, WANT, NO, GO, DONE — always visible and always accessible. Covers multiple SIB functions with minimal vocabulary.

AAC Materials / Core Word Boards

Stable, consistent, always present — works when verbal language is offline. The core vocabulary board provides coverage across multiple SIB functions simultaneously, meaning a child whose function shifts across contexts has a single tool that adapts.
This is the go-to upgrade when a child has mastered single-message devices and is ready for multi-function communication.

High-Tech AAC Device / Tablet AAC App
What It Is
Dedicated speech-generating device or tablet with AAC app featuring a large one-touch emergency message on the home screen. Speaks for the child instantly and unambiguously.

🔵 Material 5
Emotion & Sensation Visual Scale
What It Is
A 1–5 illustrated scale from "CALM" to "CRISIS" paired with a body map for pain location pointing. Child points to their current state — no words required.
Canon Category
Visual Supports / Regulation Scales
Price Range
₹100–1,000 | DIY available (₹0) — drawn by hand with colored circles and face sketches. Child's pointing is the mechanism — illustration quality is irrelevant.
Why It Works
Externalizes internal states that have no words. Allows caregivers to respond before SIB becomes necessary — intervening at a level 3 escalation rather than waiting for a level 5 crisis.
The emotion scale also builds interoception — the child's ability to recognize their own internal states — which is a prerequisite for self-regulation. It is both an FCT tool and a long-term self-advocacy skill.

🟣 Material 6
Choice Board for Immediate Needs
What It Is
A board with real photographs of the child's most common wants — foods, activities, people, sensory tools. The child points to what they need. No word-finding required.
Canon Category
Visual Supports / Choice Systems
Price Range
₹200–1,500 | DIY available (real photos, ₹0) — actual photos of the child's real preferred items work best anyway. The specificity of real photographs outperforms generic symbols.
Why It Works
Eliminates frustrated guessing — the most common driver of tangible-maintained SIB. No word-finding required. Immediate need expression → immediate provision.
When SIB is tangible-maintained (the child wants something specific and can't communicate it), the choice board is often the single most effective FCT tool because it directly addresses the communication gap causing the crisis.

🟤 Material 7
Touch-Based Communication Signals
What It Is
Agreed-upon touch patterns: 1 tap = help / 2 squeezes = stop / gentle stroke = stay with me. Require no devices, no symbols, and cannot be lost, forgotten, or run out of battery.
Canon Category
Communication Systems / Body-Based AAC
Price Range
₹0 (free) — requires training and practice only.
Why It Works
Always available — the child always has their hands. Works in dark or chaotic environments where visual tools fail. Works when devices are uncharged or unavailable.
Touch signals are the ultimate backup system — always online, always accessible, zero cost. They are particularly powerful for attention-maintained SIB, where the child needs physical connection. The signal replaces the SIB as a body-based request for closeness.
Requires all caregivers to learn and honor the same signals consistently.
⚫ Material 8
Environmental Modification Cue Cards
What It Is
Cards reading "TOO LOUD," "TOO BRIGHT," "NEED SPACE," "NEED MOVEMENT" — the child presents the card, the environment changes immediately. Direct control over sensory experience.
Canon Category
Visual Supports / Environmental Communication
Price Range
₹100–1,000 | DIY available — paper + marker + laminating pouch. Symbol recognizability matters; quality of paper does not.
Why It Works
Gives children direct control over sensory triggers that drive SIB. Communication causes environmental change — the most powerful FCT experience possible: the child learns that their communication reshapes the world around them.
For sensory-maintained or automatic-function SIB, environmental cue cards are often more effective than social communication tools, because they address the sensory experience directly. The environment changes because the child spoke. That is profound.

Caregiver Response Training Materials
What It Is
Quick-reference guides, response scripts, and function-based protocol cards for all caregivers in the child's life — parents, grandparents, teachers, domestic help, siblings.

Why It Works
Communication tools only work if caregivers respond. This is the other half of the FCT system — and the half most often overlooked.
Inconsistent caregiver response is the primary reason FCT fails. One person who ignores the communication tool resets weeks of progress. Every adult in the child's life must respond identically, immediately, and every single time.

FCT Is Safe. But SIB Requires Professional Assessment Before Home Implementation.
🔴 DO NOT PROCEED — Seek Professional Consultation
  • SIB involves open wounds, bone/joint injury risk, or medical emergency
  • SIB is escalating rapidly despite previous communication attempts
  • SIB function has NOT been identified through professional FBA
  • Child has not been medically evaluated to rule out pain, GI, dental, or infection
  • SIB occurs exclusively when alone (possible automatic/sensory function)
  • Child is under 2 years old — requires professional developmental assessment
🟡 PROCEED WITH CAUTION
  • First week of implementing: expect SIB to temporarily increase (extinction burst)
  • Child shows severe distress when communication attempt is not immediately honored
  • Multiple caregivers not yet trained — pause until all key adults are aligned
  • Child's language development is atypical in ways you don't fully understand
🟢 SAFE TO PROCEED
  • SIB function has been identified (escape / attention / tangible / sensory-internal)
  • Medical causes have been ruled out
  • All primary caregivers have been briefed on the protocol
  • Simple, immediate-response communication tool is in place
  • Child is in a relatively stable health state

Safety note on extinction burst: When you begin honoring communication and stopping responding to SIB, SIB may initially increase before it decreases. This is a normal behavioral process — it means the FCT is working. Stay consistent. Contact your BCBA if the burst is severe.

FCT Doesn't Happen in a Therapy Room. It Happens Everywhere.
FCT does not require a special space. It requires a consistent, accessible communication system available in every space. The setup is about positioning communication tools — not a room.
Kitchen
Core vocabulary board at child's eye height. Choice board for food items within reach. Break card on refrigerator door. Caregiver quick-reference guide posted visibly.
Living Room
Communication device charged on side table at all times. Emotion scale on wall at pointing height. Environmental cue cards in basket within child's reach. Soft landing zone available.
Bedroom
Simple 3-item choice board for bedtime routine. Touch signal prompts visible for parent. Communication tool within reach of bed for nighttime needs.
Out-of-Home
Break card laminated on wristband or lanyard. Portable choice board on key ring. Communication device charged and in bag before departure.

Universal rule: Communication tools must be accessible BEFORE distress occurs — not retrieved during crisis. All adults in the space must know the child's communication system. Caregiver must be within response distance during high-risk periods.

Step 1 of 6
🟢 The Invitation | 30–60 seconds
The Invitation
What you're doing: Bringing the child into awareness of the communication tool — not demanding they use it. No pressure. No performance.
The Exact Words to Say
"Hey, look what I have here. This says [message]. Want to see how it works?"
Show the device/card. Press it yourself. Let the child observe. Wait 5–10 seconds after showing — don't fill the silence.
Body Language
  • Get down to the child's physical level
  • Calm, warm face — no urgency, no anxiety
  • Offer the tool at arm's length — don't thrust it forward
What Acceptance Looks Like
  • Child glances at or reaches toward the tool
  • Child presses/touches it when shown how
  • Child stays in the space rather than moving away
  • Any social orienting response
What Resistance Looks Like
  • Moves away: Follow gently. Even proximity counts today.
  • Ignores: "I'm going to put this here in case you want it." No demand.
  • Pushes away: "Okay, here it is anyway." Keep available, remove the demand.

Pairing principle: This first contact happens during a calm, preferred moment — NOT during distress. The child must associate the tool with positive, low-demand contexts before it becomes useful during crisis.
Step 2 of 6
🔵 The Engagement | 1–3 minutes
The Engagement
What you're doing: Introducing the communication tool during a calm, non-distressing moment. You are teaching the tool before the child needs it in crisis.
For Single-Message Device (Big Mack)
  1. Model pressing it yourself: "Watch me. I press this, and it says [message]."
  1. Guide hand to press: "Your turn." Provide hand-over-hand if needed.
  1. Immediately respond: "You said you need a break! Great — let's take one."
  1. Repeat 2–3 times across a relaxed context.
For Break Card
  1. Show the card: "This card means 'stop' or 'I need a break.'"
  1. Practice the exchange: child hands card, you stop immediately.
  1. Return the card: "Keep this one. You can use it whenever you need."
For Core Vocabulary Board
  1. Point to STOP: "This one says 'stop.'" Point to HELP: "This one says 'help.'"
  1. Ask in a game format: "Can you show me where 'want' is?"
  1. Model use: "Watch — I want something. I point to WANT." Then provide something fun.

Reinforcement cue: Any contact with the communication tool gets immediate, enthusiastic praise: "YES! You used your voice!" Engagement = excellent. Tolerance = good start. Avoidance = pause, reduce demand, try tomorrow.
Step 3 of 6
🟠 The Therapeutic Action — FCT In The Moment
FCT in the Moment
This step is different from all others. It does not happen during a calm practice session. It happens the moment you see the earliest signs of distress building — before the SIB, not after.
Tier 1 — Proactive Prompt
Earliest distress signs (Level 2). Parent points to communication tool. "Show me on this — what do you need?" Wait 5 seconds. If child uses tool: respond immediately. If not: name the function and provide it.
Tier 2 — Active Prompt
Distress building (Level 3), SIB not yet begun. Bring tool to child. Physically guide if needed. IMMEDIATELY honor the message: "You said stop. We stop RIGHT NOW."
Tier 3 — Post-SIB Recovery
After SIB, once child is calm (Level 1–2). Revisit communication tool in neutral way. "Next time, you can show me this instead." No lecture. Return to calm activity.
The Golden Rule of FCT: Communication must work BETTER than SIB to replace it. When the child presses "I need a break" → break must happen faster and more reliably than head-hitting ever produced one. Speed and certainty of response IS the intervention.
Step 4 of 6
🟡 Repeat & Vary | Target: 3–5 successful exchanges per day
Repeat & Vary
FCT is not a scheduled 20-minute activity. It is woven into every context where the SIB function occurs. Each day, aim for 3–5 successful exchanges where the child used the communication tool (even with prompting), the caregiver responded immediately, and the exchange produced the outcome the child needed.
"3 good exchanges are worth more than 30 forced attempts."

Satiation Signals — Time to Stop for Today
  • Child begins throwing or damaging communication tool
  • Child begins ignoring tool even with prompting
  • Child's distress level has been at 4–5 for extended period without recovery
  • Caregiver is no longer able to respond calmly
Step 5 of 6
🌟 Reinforce & Celebrate | Within 3 seconds
Reinforce & Celebrate
The single most important rule in FCT: Respond to communication EVERY TIME. Immediately. With enthusiasm. The child will only continue using communication instead of SIB if communication is undeniably more effective.
Break card used:
"YES! You showed me the break card! We're taking a break RIGHT NOW. I'm so proud of you for telling me."
Help button pressed:
"You asked for help! Great — I'm right here." [Provide help immediately]
Emotion scale at level 4:
"You're showing me you're almost at the top. Thank you for telling me. Let's [calming strategy]."
"Too loud" card handed:
"Too loud! Got it." [Reduce volume immediately — no delay]

"Celebrate the attempt, not just the success."

Step 6 of 6
🌊 The Cool-Down | 2–5 minutes post-exchange
The Cool-Down
After a successful communication exchange, the child's nervous system needs a regulated landing. This cool-down period builds a powerful association: "When I communicate, I get what I need AND I feel calm. The communication works AND it's safe."
Transition Warning
"We're almost done here. One more minute, then we move to [next activity]." Pair with visual timer showing 1-minute countdown.
Sensory Cool-Down (60–90 seconds)
Proprioceptive: tight hug, wall push-ups. Vestibular: slow rhythmic rocking. Tactile: hand pressure, textured toy. Auditory: favorite song at low volume.
Communication Tool Put-Away Ritual
"We're done with the break card for now. Let's put it right here so it's ready for next time." Child places it in designated spot. The tool is always available — it never disappears.
Transition to Next Activity
"Good work telling me what you needed. Now let's [preferred activity]." If child resists ending, honor 1–2 additional minutes — don't force transition when nervous system is still settling.
60 Seconds of Data Now Saves Weeks of Guessing Later.
Consistent data collection is the difference between knowing your FCT is working and hoping it is. By end of week 2, you should see communication tool use increasing (with prompting), SIB frequency beginning to plateau, and your response latency decreasing.
📊 Track 3 Things
  1. Communication Tool Used — which material the child actually adopted today
  1. SIB Occurrence — Yes / No / Partial (began but redirected)
  1. Response Latency — Immediate <3 sec / Delayed 3–10 sec / Late >10 sec
🔍 Why These Three Metrics
  • Tool used → reveals which tools the child actually adopts
  • SIB occurrence → the primary outcome measure of FCT effectiveness
  • Response latency → if SIB persists despite communication attempts, slow response is often the culprit

Most FCT Sessions Don't Go Perfectly. Here's What Actually Happened and What to Do.
❓ Child used tool but SIB still occurred
Why: Caregiver response was too slow or didn't match the function. Fix: Speed up response. If child pressed "break" and you offered a different activity instead of an actual break, the function wasn't met. Match precisely.
❓ Child has never once touched the communication tool
Why: Tool was introduced during distress, not during calm. No positive pairing exists yet. Fix: Return to Step 1. Use the tool yourself. Introduce only during fun, low-demand moments for 3–5 days first.
❓ SIB got WORSE after starting FCT
Why: May be an extinction burst (normal) or wrong FCT target function. Fix: If burst lasts 3–5 days then decreases — stay consistent. If escalating past Day 7 — contact your BCBA. The functional hypothesis may need revision.
❓ Child uses tool at home but not at school
Why: School caregivers have not been trained or don't respond consistently. Fix: Train school staff using the teacher communication template (Card 37). Request a joint meeting. FCT only works where it's consistently honored.
❓ Different family members respond differently
Why: Inconsistent caregiver response is the most common FCT failure point. Fix: Family meeting. Caregiver Quick Reference Guide. Everyone uses identical responses. No exceptions.
❓ Child abandoned the break card after initial use
Why: The card stopped being honored reliably. Fix: Recommit to 100% immediate honoring for 2 additional weeks. The card lost credibility — it needs to be re-established as more reliable than SIB.
❓ Session ended in a severe SIB episode
Why: Distress exceeded communication system capacity. Fix: Safety first. After resolution: no debriefing or lecturing. Return to calm normalcy. Note the trigger for future antecedent modification. Today was data, not failure.
No Two Children Communicate the Same Way. No FCT Program Looks Identical.
The FCT difficulty slider lets you adjust in real time — pulling toward Easier on hard days and new contexts, moving toward Harder as skills consolidate.
Child Profile
FCT Adaptation
Primarily nonverbal
Lean heavily on physical tools (button, card). Touch signals as backup. No verbal prompting during distress.
Verbal but language collapses under stress
Dual-channel system: verbal attempt + physical tool always available. Don't remove verbal option — provide physical backup.
High sensory sensitivity
Environmental cue cards are most critical. Address sensory SIB triggers alongside communication.
Strong visual learner
Core vocabulary board + choice boards. Heavy visual support throughout all contexts.
Low motor control / tremor
Simple large-target tools only (Big Mack > multi-symbol board). Eye gaze systems if available.
Week 1–2: Do Not Look for Dramatic Change. Look for These Specific Things.
████░░░░░░░░░░ Week 1–2 | ~15% of Expected Progress
✅ What You WILL Likely See
  • Child tolerates presence of communication tool without refusing it
  • Child contacts or approaches tool when prompted during calm practice
  • 1–2 instances of spontaneous or prompted tool use (even one counts enormously)
  • SIB may temporarily increase (extinction burst) — this means FCT is working
  • You are responding faster to communication attempts
✗ What You Will NOT See Yet (Normal)
  • Spontaneous, unprompted tool use during high distress
  • Measurable SIB decline (too early)
  • Child using tool across multiple settings independently
  • Generalization to non-trained partners

"If your child contacts the communication tool one time today — voluntarily or with guidance — that is real, measurable, neurologically significant progress."
Week 3–4: The Child's Nervous System Is Beginning to Trust the New Communication Pathway.
████████░░░░░░ Week 3–4 | ~40% of Expected Progress
Earlier Intervention
Child begins approaching communication tool BEFORE full distress peak — earlier and earlier in the escalation curve
SIB Plateau
SIB frequency shows a measurable plateau — not yet declining, but no longer climbing
30%+ Tool Use
Child uses communication tool in 30%+ of SIB-risk contexts — even with prompting
Automatic Response
Caregiver response has become automatic — response latency under 3 seconds consistently
Social Referencing
Child begins to look at caregiver after using tool — checking for response. Social referencing emerging.
"You may notice that you're more confident too. You have a response. You're not standing there helpless. Your confidence communicates safety to your child — and a safe child communicates more."
Week 5–8: Mastery Doesn't Mean Perfection. It Means the New Pathway Is Stronger Than the Old One.
████████████░░ Week 5–8 | ~75% of Expected Progress
1. Communication Use Rate
Child uses communication tool (independently or with minimal gestural prompt) in 75%+ of instances where SIB previously occurred in targeted function
2. SIB Frequency Reduction
SIB frequency measurably reduced from baseline — minimum 40% reduction in SIB episodes in primary function context
3. Generalization
Child uses communication tool with at least 2 different partners or in at least 2 different settings
4. Independence
At least 50% of successful exchanges are self-initiated — no physical prompt needed

🏅MASTERY BADGE: When all 4 indicators are observed across 3 consecutive days → D-413 FCT Mastery Achieved. Document this date. Then proceed to D-414 (Environmental Changes for SIB) or expand FCT to a second SIB function.

FCT Is Evidence-Based. But SIB Can Have Layers. Here's When to Pause and Call.
🔴 Red Flag 1 — SIB Intensity Escalation
SIB episodes becoming more severe (not just more frequent) during FCT, past Day 7. Wounds that require medical attention. Action: Stop. Contact BCBA and pediatrician today.
🔴 Red Flag 2 — Medical Symptoms
SIB accompanied by crying at unusual times, holding ear/jaw/stomach, disrupted sleep, appetite changes, fever. Action: Medical evaluation before continuing FCT — this may be pain communication.
🔴 Red Flag 3 — New SIB Topography
Child developing new forms of SIB (was head-hitting; now also biting self, or new self-injury site). Action: New functional assessment may be needed — different function may be driving the new topography.
🔴 Red Flag 4 — Communication System Collapse
Child was using tool successfully; abruptly stopped and SIB dramatically increased. Action: Check for environmental change (school transition? family change? medical issue?) and contact your support team.
🔴 Red Flag 5 — Caregiver Distress
Primary caregiver's mental health is deteriorating. Consistent, calm response is no longer possible. Action: Caregiver needs support first. FCT cannot be delivered by a caregiver in crisis. Call helpline.
🔴 Red Flag 6 — No FCT Response After 4 Weeks
Zero SIB reduction and zero increase in communication tool use despite consistent implementation. Action: FCT function hypothesis may be incorrect. Request professional FBA review.

Three Families. Three Functions. One Outcome: Communication That Doesn't Require Pain.
Rohan, age 5 — Hyderabad | Escape-Maintained SIB
Before: Rohan hit his head against the wall whenever a task felt too hard or ran too long. Nothing was consistent and we always felt one step behind.
After 8 weeks with Big Mack programmed to "I need a break": Head-hitting dropped by 70% within 6 weeks. He presses the button now — sometimes twice, he's so enthusiastic about it working.
Therapist note (BCBA): The breakthrough came in Week 4 when he pressed it unprompted in the middle of a demanding task. He looked at me after. He knew he had a voice.
Diya, age 7 — Mumbai | Attention-Maintained SIB
Before: Diya would scratch her arms whenever I was on the phone or in the next room. We spent months on sensory interventions that helped somewhat but never reached the core pattern.
After touch signals + "I need you" visual card: A one-tap signal on my arm replaced the scratching in most contexts within 5 weeks. The relief she shows when I respond immediately — she lights up.
Therapist note (SLP + BCBA): The touch signal worked because it required even less effort than the scratching and produced faster, warmer caregiver response. Function match is everything.
Arjun, age 9 — Bengaluru | Dual-Function SIB
Before: Two completely different SIB patterns that looked the same from outside. The FBA revealed two functions — sometimes escape, sometimes tangible.
After dual-tool system (choice board + break card): Took 10 weeks. But SIB dropped by 85%. He now uses both tools in different contexts and has started building full AAC.
Therapist note (BCBA): Dual-function SIB requires dual-tool FCT. The FBA was non-negotiable — without it, we would have been guessing for months.
Outcomes vary. All vignettes are illustrative composites from Pinnacle clinical data. Individual results depend on SIB function, intensity, and implementation fidelity.
